L25: # Wider Edge Lines
L26: 
L27: 【5†Image: U.S. Department of Transportation logo】U.S. Department of Transportation
L28: Federal Highway Administration
L29: FHWA-SA-21-055
L30: 
L31:   * 【6†Image: PDF】【7†Wider Edge Lines_508.pdf (PDF, 150.16 KB)】
L32: Roadway departures account for over half of all traffic fatalities in the United States. If drivers cannot clearly identify the edge of the travel lanes and see the road alignment ahead, the risk of roadway departure may be greater. Wider edge lines enhance the visibility of travel lane boundaries compared to traditional edge lines. Edge lines are considered ”wider“ when the marking width is increased from the minimum normal line width of 4 inches to the maximum normal line width of 6 inches.^{【8†1】}
L33: 【9†Image: "A two-lane undivided roadway marked with a double yellow centerline and solid white edge line. The solid white edge line in the foreground of the image is visibility wider than the centerline markings."】
L34: 
L35: Source: Texas Transportation Institute
L36: ## Applications
L37: Wider edge lines increase drivers’ perception of the edge of the travel lane and can provide a safety benefit to all facility types (e.g., freeways, multilane divided and undivided highways, two-lane highways) in both urban and rural areas.^{【8†2】} Wider edge lines are most effective in reducing crashes on rural two-lane highways, especially for single-vehicle crashes.^{【8†3】} Agencies should also consider implementing a systemic approach to wider edge line installation based roadway departure crash risk factors.
L38: Potential risk factors for two-lane rural roads include:
L39:   * Pavement and shoulder widths.
L40:   * Presence of curves.
L41:   * Traffic volumes.
L42:   * History of nighttime crashes.
L43: ## Considerations
L44:   * Wider edge lines are relatively low cost.
L45:   * Wider edge lines can be implemented using existing equipment during maintenance procedures like re-striping and resurfacing, with the only cost increase being the additional material.
L46:   * Paint may have a lower initial cost, but more durable materials (e.g., thermoplastic) may result in a lower life cycle cost based on their longer service life.
L47:   * As the number of automated vehicles increases on roadways, wider edge lines may provide better guidance for these vehicles’ sensors.
